title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 4: Uphold the Constitution
keywords: rare is the opportunity for greatness
primary_topics: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2) -- CJP's December 20, 2009 Inquirer column on a jurist's duty to uphold the Constitution over personal gratitude to the appointing President, framed by a new magistrate's question about reconciling the two

His answer, anchored in his own David v. Arroyo concurrence: the best way to show gratitude is to choose 'a lasting legacy' over 'shortsighted gains,' for justices take an oath to the Constitution and (paraphrasing Quezon) 'gratitude to the President ends where duty to the Constitution and the people begins'

His warning of 'hesitation and vacillation' in how the Court was handling the petitions against PP 1959 (Maguindanao martial law) -- the 20-day comment period that would breach the 30-day decision deadline, and a Dec. 15 resolution adding five issues, some never raised by the parties

His exhortation that the Court not 'cower or cop-out or hide behind legalisms,' nor 'invent legal excuses' out of a 'false sense of gratitude': 'Rare is the opportunity for greatness. Let the Court not squander the moment.'
sub_topics: The new magistrate's question: how to reconcile gratitude to the appointing President with opinions overturning her actions -- a question that 'nags the conscience of every new jurist,' since gratitude is a cherished Filipino value

CJP's answer in two parts: he hands the magistrate his David v. Arroyo (May 3, 2006) concurrence nullifying the 'extraneous' provisions of PP 1017 (which echoed Marcos's PP 1081), quoting its warning that the country might have been spared dictatorship had the Court of that era reminded the president of 'the inevitable historical damnation of despots and tyrants'

The principle: sometimes the best gratitude is to cast aside 'shortsighted gains' for a 'lasting legacy'; justices swear to uphold the Constitution and, on entering the Court, become 'a god of the law, beholden only to blindfolded justice' -- and, paraphrasing Quezon, 'gratitude to the President ends where duty to the Constitution and the people begins'

The PP 1959 worry: the Constitution gives the Court only 30 days from the Dec. 7 filing to decide, yet on Dec. 8 it merely asked for comment without oral argument, and on Dec. 15 (after GMA lifted the proclamation) ordered 20 days of comment on whether the lifting mooted the petitions -- a timetable that could no longer meet the 30-day mandate

The five added issues: whether 'rebellion' here means the same as in the Penal Code; whether PP 1959 authorized warrantless arrests/searches/seizures; whether martial law is a 'joint and sequential function' of President and Congress leaving the Court 'nothing to review' once lifted; whether the Court's review can run simultaneously with Congress's power to revoke (and which prevails); and whether the Court's judgment on the factual basis is essential to the validity of related acts
The danger: some of these issues 'were never raised by the parties' and 'can be cleverly turned to mangle the high-minded constitutional safeguards against creeping authoritarianism'

The exhortation: 'The Court faces a historic moment. It cannot cower or cop-out or hide behind legalisms,' nor invent excuses from 'a false sense of gratitude' -- 'Rare is the opportunity for greatness. Let the Court not squander the moment'

Handing over his own opinion: he answers by giving the magistrate a copy of his David v. Arroyo concurrence, pointing to its closing warning that the country might have escaped dictatorship had the Court of Marcos's day reminded him of 'the inevitable historical damnation of despots and tyrants.'
'A god of the law': he describes how a lawyer entering 'the inner sanctum' leaves behind 'all humanity' to become 'a god of the law, beholden only to blindfolded justice.'

The five smuggled issues: he flags that the Court's Dec. 15 resolution raised questions 'never raised by the parties' that could be 'cleverly turned to mangle' the safeguards against 'creeping authoritarianism.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's December 20, 2009 Inquirer column, opens with a newly appointed magistrate's question that 'nags the conscience of every new jurist': how to reconcile gratitude to the President who appointed him with opinions overturning her actions, gratitude being a cherished Filipino value. CJP answers in two moves. First, he hands the magistrate his own David v. Arroyo (2006) concurrence -- which nullified the 'extraneous' provisions of PP 1017 that echoed Marcos's PP 1081 -- and points to its warning that the country might have been spared dictatorship had the Court of that era reminded the president of 'the inevitable historical damnation of despots and tyrants.' Second, he explains that the best gratitude is to choose a 'lasting legacy' over 'shortsighted gains': justices swear to uphold the Constitution and, entering the inner sanctum, become 'a god of the law, beholden only to blindfolded justice,' so that, paraphrasing Quezon, 'gratitude to the President ends where duty to the Constitution and the people begins.' He then turns to a live worry -- 'hesitation and vacillation' in how the Court was treating the petitions against PP 1959 (Maguindanao martial law). The Constitution gave it only 30 days from the Dec. 7 filing, yet it merely asked for comment without oral argument and, after GMA lifted the proclamation, ordered 20 days of comment on whether the lifting mooted the case -- a schedule that could no longer meet the deadline -- while a Dec. 15 resolution raised five further issues, some 'never raised by the parties,' that 'can be cleverly turned to mangle the... safeguards against creeping authoritarianism.' The Court, he concludes, 'faces a historic moment' and must not 'cower or cop-out or hide behind legalisms' or invent excuses from 'a false sense of gratitude': 'Rare is the opportunity for greatness. Let the Court not squander the moment.'
